title: Use a Graphical User Interface (GUI)-based spreadsheet application to solve a given problem

lessons.title: Spreadsheet basics
lessons.html:
Spreadsheet basics

A spreadsheet application, such as Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc, is a program that organises numbers and text in a grid. It is called GUI-based because you work with windows, menus, buttons and a mouse. In a seed laboratory or on a farm, spreadsheets are used for test results, germination calculations, stock lists, trial data and costs.

The parts of a spreadsheet

  • Workbook: the whole file.
  • Worksheet: one page or tab in the workbook, for example 'January' or 'Germination'.
  • Columns are labelled with letters (A, B, C...). Rows are numbered (1, 2, 3...).
  • Cell: the box where a column and row meet. Its address is like B4.
  • Formula bar: shows what is really in the selected cell.
  • Ribbon or menu: buttons for formatting, inserting charts and more.

Setting up a good table

  1. Put a clear title at the top.
  2. Put column headings in row 1 or 2, for example Sample number, Crop, Lot, Normal seedlings, Abnormal, Dead, Germination %.
  3. Enter one record per row, for example one sample per row.
  4. Do not leave empty rows in the middle of the data.
  5. Use the same format in each column, such as dates as dates and numbers as numbers.

Saving your work

Save the workbook with a clear name, such as Germination_Results_2026_Oct, in the correct folder. Save often. Keep backups as your workplace requires. Do not keep the only copy of important data on a flash drive.

Formatting

Make headings bold, set column widths so text fits, and set the number of decimal places. Use borders and shading lightly, so the sheet is easy to read.

lessons.title: Formulas and functions
lessons.html:
Formulas and functions

The power of a spreadsheet is that it calculates for you. When a number changes, the answer updates automatically.

Writing a formula

Every formula starts with an equals sign (=). Use cell addresses, not the numbers themselves.

OperationExample
Add=B2+C2
Subtract=B2-C2
Multiply=B2*C2
Divide=B2/C2

Useful functions

  • =SUM(B2:B20) adds all values in a range.
  • =AVERAGE(B2:E2) gives the average, for example of four germination replicates.
  • =MAX() and =MIN() give the highest and lowest values.
  • =COUNT() counts cells with numbers.
  • =ROUND(F2,0) rounds a value to whole numbers.
  • =IF(F2<85,"Below","OK") checks a condition, for example whether germination is below a company standard.

Example: germination percentage

If 100 seeds were planted per replicate and normal seedlings for four replicates are in B2 to E2, the average germination percentage in F2 is =AVERAGE(B2:E2). Copy the formula down by dragging the fill handle, and the spreadsheet adjusts the row numbers for each sample.

Absolute references

Sometimes a formula must always point to one cell, for example a price per kilogram in cell H1. Use a dollar sign: =B2*$H$1. When copied down, $H$1 stays fixed.

Checking formulas

Check one or two answers by hand or calculator. Look out for error messages such as #DIV/0! (dividing by zero) or #VALUE! (text where a number should be).

Never type an answer over a formula cell. If you overwrite a formula with a number, the sheet will no longer update when the data changes, and nobody may notice the mistake. Click on a cell and look at the formula bar to see whether it holds a formula or a typed value.

lessons.title: Sorting, charts and printing to solve a problem
lessons.html:
Sorting, charts and printing to solve a problem

A spreadsheet is used to answer a question. For example: which seed lots this month had germination below the company standard, and how do the cultivars compare?

Steps to solve a problem

  1. Understand the question. What answer is needed and for whom?
  2. Collect the data and enter it accurately, one record per row.
  3. Calculate with formulas, for example average germination per lot.
  4. Sort and filter to find what you need.
  5. Present the answer with a summary table or chart.
  6. Check the results make sense.

Sorting and filtering

  • Select the table and use Sort to order it, for example from lowest to highest germination.
  • Use Filter to show only some rows, for example only maize, or only lots marked 'Below'.
  • Always select the whole table before sorting, or rows will be mixed up and data will be wrong.

Charts

Charts make numbers easy to understand. Select the data and insert a chart:

  • Column chart to compare values, such as average germination per cultivar.
  • Line chart to show change over time, such as monthly sample numbers.
  • Pie chart only to show parts of a whole.

Give every chart a title and axis labels.

Printing

Use Print Preview. Set landscape or portrait, fit the table to one page wide, and add a header with the title and date. Print only what is needed.

Protecting data

Keep test results confidential. Use passwords where required and do not e-mail client data to unauthorised people.

Key points

  • A workbook has worksheets made of rows, columns and cells.
  • Put one record per row with clear column headings.
  • Formulas start with = and use cell addresses; functions like SUM and AVERAGE save time.
  • Select the whole table before sorting.
  • Use labelled charts to present answers and check results make sense.
